The Simple Definition First

"The great unwashed" is a phrase used to describe ordinary, common people — especially those from the lower or working classes — in a condescending, snobbish way. When someone uses this phrase, they are looking down on a large group of people and suggesting that those people are uneducated, unsophisticated, or beneath them socially.

Think of it this way: if a wealthy politician privately says "I don't care what the great unwashed think about my policies," they are dismissing ordinary citizens as unimportant people whose opinions don't matter.
Breaking It Down Word by Word

"Great" here doesn't mean "wonderful" or "excellent." It means large in number — a great (huge) crowd of people. So it's saying: a massive, countless group.

"Unwashed" literally means people who haven't bathed or cleaned themselves. But in this phrase, it carries a figurative meaning — it means people who are perceived as rough, crude, unrefined, or lacking in good manners and education.

Put them together: a vast multitude of common, unrefined people.

To truly understand this phrase, you need to travel back in time to 19th-century Britain. This context is everything.

In the 1800s, taking a bath regularly was not something most people could easily do. During periods of rapid industrialization and urbanization, overcrowding and poor sanitation were rampant. Poor people living in cramped cities had very little access to clean water, soap, or proper bathing facilities. Bathing was genuinely expensive and difficult for the working classes.

The wealthy, on the other hand, could afford hot water, servants, and private bathing rooms. So being clean — being washed — was actually a sign of wealth and status. It told the world that you were privileged enough to afford hygiene.

This created a cruel social divide: rich people were literally cleaner than poor people, not because the poor chose to be dirty, but because poverty made cleanliness difficult. The upper classes then used this physical difference as a weapon — a way to mock and belittle the masses.

So the word "unwashed" stopped just meaning not bathed. It became a shorthand for being low class, rough, and inferior. The phrase quickly evolved to become a metaphor for the masses — those without wealth, education, or social standing.

Though attributed by many to the philosopher Edmund Burke, the first confirmed published use of the phrase was by the writer Edward Bulwer-Lytton in 1830, in a dedicatory epistle for his novel Paul Clifford.

The relevant passage reads: "He is certainly a man who bathes and 'lives cleanly', (two especial charges preferred against him by Messrs. the Great Unwashed)." Lytton uses the phrase to highlight the hypocrisy of a society that prioritises superficial cleanliness over genuine social justice.

In plain English, this passage is satirical — it's mocking the upper classes for judging a man harshly simply because he was clean. The "charges" (accusations) being brought against him by "the Great Unwashed" were that he bathed and lived decently. It was Bulwer-Lytton's way of holding up a mirror to the absurd snobbery of the era.

The noun sense of "the lower class" (also great unwashed) is first recorded in print from 1830.
How Other Famous Writers Used It

Once Bulwer-Lytton popularised the phrase, other great writers of the era picked it up.

William Makepeace Thackeray used it in his novel The History of Pendennis (1848–1850), writing: "Gentlemen, there can be but little doubt that your ancestors were the Great Unwashed: and in the Temple especially, it is pretty certain, that only under the greatest difficulties and restrictions the virtue which has been pronounced to be next to godliness could have been practised at all."

Thackeray's use is interesting because here he is actually addressing wealthy, educated gentlemen and reminding them that their own ancestors were once the great unwashed too — a dig at the pretension of the upper classes who had forgotten their humble roots.
What the Phrase Really Communicates (The Tone)

This phrase drips with condescension. When you use it seriously (not as a joke), you are doing several things at once:

You are placing yourself above others. The very act of calling people "the great unwashed" implies you are not one of them — that you stand apart from the common rabble.

You are dismissing people as a nameless mass. The phrase doesn't see individuals. It lumps millions of people together into one faceless, inferior blob.

You are linking poverty to moral failure. This is perhaps its ugliest quality. It implies that being poor, uneducated, or ordinary is somehow a character flaw — that people are "low" because they deserve to be.

The phrase signifies a social and political divide, a separation between those in power and those subjected to it.

Understanding "the great unwashed" becomes even clearer when you compare it to similar phrases that carry the same meaning:

"The masses" — a more neutral term for ordinary people in large numbers. Less insulting in tone.

"Hoi polloi" — a Greek phrase (meaning "the many") used to refer to common people. It is considered synonymous with "the great unwashed," indicating a broad grouping of ordinary folks often dismissed by the elite.

"The common people" or "the rabble" — similar in meaning, with "rabble" being especially dismissive.

"The plebs" (or "plebeians") — from ancient Rome, where plebeians were the common citizens as opposed to the aristocratic patricians. Now used casually to mean common, ordinary people.

All of these terms share the same DNA: they draw a line between an elite "us" and a common, inferior "them."
How the Meaning Has Shifted Over Time

The phrase has not stayed frozen since 1830. Over time, it has evolved in how people use and understand it.

Originally: It was used earnestly by the upper classes to genuinely look down on the poor and working class.

Later: Writers and thinkers began using it ironically — meaning they used it while secretly mocking the snobbishness behind it, not the poor people themselves. Thackeray's use above is a perfect example.

Today: The phrase is now mostly used in three ways:

  1. Sarcastically or humorously — to poke fun at elitism. Someone might say "Oh, I'm sure the great unwashed won't notice the difference" while laughing at themselves for sounding like a snob.
  2. Self-deprecatingly — a person might call themselves part of the great unwashed as a humble, funny way of saying they're just an ordinary person.
  3. As genuine snobbery — yes, some people still use it sincerely, and when they do, it reveals a lot about their attitude toward others.

In contemporary discussions about class and culture, the phrase is often used to highlight the gap between a privileged minority and the general populace. For example, a politician might disparage populist movements by claiming they are fuelled by the grievances of "the great unwashed." Conversely, activists might reclaim the term in a proudly populist context.

Here are clear examples to show you how the phrase works in practice:

  • "The CEO never mingled with the great unwashed; he had his own private elevator and dining room." (Used seriously — showing his snobbery.)
  • "Oh, don't worry about me — I'm just one of the great unwashed trying to get a good deal." (Used humorously and self-deprecatingly.)
  • "The old guard of the party dismissed the new voters as the great unwashed, which is exactly why they lost the election." (Used to criticise someone's arrogance.)

"The great unwashed" is a phrase born from class inequality. It started as a literal observation (poor people couldn't wash easily) and became a lasting metaphor for how elites look down on ordinary people.

What makes it powerful as a phrase — and what has kept it alive for nearly 200 years — is that it captures something timeless: the tendency of those in power to view the masses not as individuals, but as an undifferentiated, inferior crowd. Every time the phrase is used, whether seriously or ironically, it echoes that long history of social division.

Knowing this phrase means knowing a little piece of how class, power, and language have always been intertwined.
